subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Starch is a large carbohydrate. What smaller molecules is it made from?
questions.explain: Carbohydrates such as starch are made up of simple sugar units like glucose.

questions.q: In the emulsion (ethanol) test, a positive result for lipids is:
questions.explain: Adding ethanol then water to a lipid produces a cloudy white emulsion.

questions.q: A positive Biuret test for protein is shown by a colour change from:
questions.explain: Biuret reagent (blue) turns purple/lilac when protein is present.

questions.q: When an enzyme is denatured, what has happened to its active site?
options: It has been killed and is now dead
It has changed shape so the substrate no longer fits
It has become larger to fit more substrate
It has joined permanently with the product
questions.explain: Denaturing changes the shape of the active site so the substrate can no longer fit; the enzyme is not 'killed' as it was never alive.

questions.q: Each enzyme works on only one type of substrate. This is because:
options: The shape of the active site is complementary to one substrate
All enzymes are the same shape
Enzymes only work at one temperature
questions.explain: The active site has a specific shape that only fits a particular substrate, giving enzymes their specificity.

questions.q: Proteins are broken down by protease enzymes into:
questions.explain: Proteases digest proteins into amino acids.

questions.q: Which statement about enzymes after they catalyse a reaction is correct?
options: They are permanently changed into the product
They are unchanged and can be reused
They are used up and must be remade
questions.explain: As catalysts, enzymes are not used up and can catalyse further reactions.

questions.q: Which enzyme breaks down starch, and into what?
questions.explain: Carbohydrases such as amylase break down starch into simple sugars.

questions.q: Why does each enzyme only catalyse one type of reaction?
options: Each enzyme is used up after one reaction
The active site is a specific shape that only fits one substrate
Enzymes only work at one temperature in the whole body
questions.explain: Enzyme specificity comes from the specific shape of the active site, which fits only its complementary substrate.

questions.q: The part of an enzyme where the substrate fits is called the:
questions.explain: The substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme, which has a complementary shape.

questions.q: Lipids (fats) are broken down by lipase into:
questions.explain: Lipase breaks lipids down into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.q: A student says 'boiling the enzyme killed it.' What is the correct scientific statement?
options: The enzyme was killed and is now dead
The enzyme used up its energy
The enzyme turned into a substrate
The enzyme was denatured, changing the active site's shape
questions.explain: Enzymes are not living, so they cannot be killed; high temperature denatures them.

questions.q: Enzymes are best described as:
options: Biological catalysts that speed up reactions
questions.explain: Enzymes are biological catalysts; they speed up reactions and are not used up.

questions.q: Which combination of food test and positive result is correct?
options: Benedict's solution turns purple with starch
Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black with starch
Biuret solution turns brick-red with protein
questions.explain: Iodine solution changes from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.

questions.q: What colour change shows a positive result when iodine solution is added to a food containing starch?
questions.explain: Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch.

questions.q: The 'lock and key' model explains that an enzyme:
options: Has an active site with a specific shape that fits a particular substrate
questions.explain: The active site has a complementary shape to its specific substrate, like a key fitting a lock.

questions.q: Why must a Biuret test for protein be carried out without heating, unlike the Benedict's test?
options: Because protein is destroyed by Benedict's solution
Because protein only forms in the cold
Because heating turns all proteins into sugars
Because the Biuret test gives its colour change at room temperature
questions.explain: The Biuret test produces a purple/lilac colour at room temperature, so heating is not required (unlike Benedict's test for sugars).

questions.q: Which food test uses Benedict's solution, and what positive result shows?
options: Test for lipid; forms a milky emulsion
Test for sugar (reducing sugar); turns from blue to brick-red/orange on heating
questions.explain: Benedict's solution, heated, turns from blue to brick-red/orange when a reducing sugar is present.

questions.q: On a graph of rate against temperature, why does the rate fall sharply after the optimum temperature?
options: The enzyme is denatured and the active site changes shape
The enzyme starts to work faster
questions.explain: Above the optimum, high temperature denatures the enzyme, changing the active site so the rate falls.

questions.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is heated well above its optimum temperature?
options: Its active site changes shape and it is denatured
questions.explain: High temperatures denature enzymes by changing the active site's shape; enzymes are not alive so cannot be 'killed'.

questions.q: Enzymes speed up reactions but are not used up themselves. This means an enzyme can:
options: Be reused to catalyse the reaction many times
Only be used once and then destroyed
questions.explain: As catalysts, enzymes are not used up in the reaction and can be used again and again.

questions.q: A student tests a food sample with Benedict's solution and heats it in a water bath. It stays blue. This shows the food:
options: Contains a lot of reducing sugar
questions.explain: Benedict's solution stays blue when no reducing sugar is present; it turns green, yellow, orange or brick-red if sugar is present.
